Import, back up & restore

Scheduled backups and two-click restores in the console, one archive with seamlessd export, seamlessd restore and import, putting ~/.seamless in git, what deleting seam.db actually costs, and moving to a new machine.

Because durable knowledge is markdown files, backup and restore are boring - and that is the feature. A release install - the installer's or Homebrew's - backs itself up every day without being asked, and the console restores any of those backups in two clicks. The rest of this page is about knowing which half of ~/.seamless is precious and which half regenerates.

Backups in the console

Settings > Backups in the console backs up the whole instance on a schedule, lists the backups it finds, and restores one. Each backup is one archive of the kind seamlessd export writes: every memory and note, a consistent snapshot of the database with your sessions, tasks, trials and projects, and a list of what each project holds. Like an export, it holds no config and no key.

The schedule

A release install (the installer's or Homebrew's) backs up every day, keeping the newest 7, in ~/.seamless/backups. A Seamless built from source backs up only once you turn it on, so a throwaway daemon never writes backups. The section's Schedule and folder card sets:

  • Back up automatically, on or off;
  • How often: every hour, every 6 hours, every day or every week. The config file can set any interval from 1h to 720h, and the list then shows it too;
  • Automatic backups to keep, from 1 to 100. Older automatic backups are deleted after the next one is written. Backups you make yourself, the safety backups taken before a restore and the updater's pre-update backups are never deleted automatically, and neither is another install's backup in a shared folder.

The first scheduled backup runs no sooner than ten minutes after Seamless starts. A run is skipped when nothing has changed since this install's newest backup in the folder (the card then says Up to date), or when the disk is short of room: a backup needs its own size free on each disk it touches, plus a reserve of 1 GiB or the backup's size, whichever is larger, so the updater can always take its own backup. Back up now makes one at once, whatever the schedule says.

What you save there wins over the config file's backup: block until you press Reset to the config file, and applies from the next backup.

The folder

Backups go to one folder you choose. Pick a synced folder or an external disk so a backup outlives the machine: the section offers the places it finds on this machine and can write to - iCloud Drive and the folders under ~/Library/CloudStorage (Dropbox, Google Drive, OneDrive) and every external disk on macOS, ~/Dropbox and the disks under /media/<you> on Linux, OneDrive and the other drives on Windows, and Seamless's own data folder everywhere. A suggestion fills in <place>/Seamless Backups.

The folder field checks the path as you type, without writing anything: Ready with the free space, Will be created, Not writable, that its disk is not connected, or Inside Seamless's data folder, which is refused (only ~/.seamless/backups itself is allowed). Saving a new folder creates it, private to your account, and tests it with a write first. The backups already in the old folder stay there.

On macOS, a folder that macOS's privacy protection keeps Seamless out of gets its own answer: allow Seamless in System Settings > Privacy & Security > Files and Folders, or give it Full Disk Access. A disk that is not connected is never written under: the run fails, says so, and the next one tries again.

The list

Available backups lists, newest first, the backups in the chosen folder and in ~/.seamless/backups, where the safety and pre-update backups always stay. Each one shows when it was made, its size and its kind in words: Automatic, Made by you, Before restore, Before updating from v0.8.1, or Exported for a file seamlessd export wrote. A backup another Seamless made says which machine it came from. What it holds opens a table of each project's memories, notes, tasks and sessions, beside how many more or fewer memories and notes the project holds now. A locked project shows its name and what the backup holds of it, never what it holds now.

Two kinds of file are listed but cannot be restored yet: an iCloud placeholder (download it in Finder first) and a backup a newer Seamless made (update to restore it). Delete removes a backup from its folder, after a confirm.

Restore, and undo

Restore… opens a card in the backup's row that compares it with now and offers two choices:

  • Replace all data with this backup. Everything goes back to how it was when the backup was made. Your current data is saved as a backup first, so you can undo it.
  • Only bring back what's missing. Adds what the backup has and this install doesn't, such as deleted memories, notes and sessions. Nothing you have now changes. A backup of memories and notes only (seamlessd export --no-db) offers just this one.

Then the card follows the restore through its steps: Checking the backup, Preparing the restored data (replace) or Saving your current data (merge), Restarting Seamless, Done, and for a replace, Saving your previous data as a backup. The heavy work happens while Seamless still serves, so a backup that fails its checks changes nothing. Seamless then restarts to finish, and agents lose it for a few seconds. Cancel restore is there until the restart.

After the restart a result card says what was restored, with Undo this restore - which opens the same card for the safety backup - and Dismiss. On Windows, Seamless cannot restart itself in place: the card asks you to run seamlessd restart within an hour. A restore that waits longer is dropped, and nothing changes.

What a restore keeps. Locks, passkeys, project privacy, repo routes and console settings stay as they are now:

  • a project locked today stays locked, and one locked in the backup comes back locked, so a restore never reduces the set of locked projects;
  • each project keeps the stricter of its privacy setting now and in the backup;
  • the passkeys and enrollment codes stay today's, so a passkey you removed after the backup does not come back;
  • the repo routes, the briefing, features, level, embeddings, update and backup settings stay this machine's;
  • every agent lease, console unlock and read grant the backup held is ended, so each agent and browser asks again;
  • with isolation requests on, the grants, moves and flows a conversation was given since the backup are kept (ended, like every grant), so a restore never shrinks what a conversation holds.

Under peer_auth with a project locked, a console restore needs a passkey, and without one the card shows the terminal command instead. seamlessd restore is the same restore without a browser.

What is precious, and what is not

seam.db holds two different kinds of thing, and conflating them is what makes people either over-protect it or under-protect it:

In seam.db If it were lost
FTS index, embeddings Rebuilt automatically from the files
Sessions, tasks, trials, events, telemetry, briefing overrides Gone - there is no file to rebuild them from

So: deleting seam.db costs you the record of what happened, not the knowledge of what is true. Every memory and note survives, because they are files.

Put it in git

The strongest backup is the one you already know how to use:

cd ~/.seamless
git init
printf 'seam.db\nseam.db-wal\nseam.db-shm\n' > .gitignore
git add . && git commit -m "seamless: initial"

Ignoring the database is deliberate. It is a binary that changes constantly, it does not diff usefully, and its contents are either rebuildable or high-churn state that a nightly commit would capture uselessly. What you want in git is the knowledge - and that diffs beautifully, because it is markdown.

Commit periodically (a cron job or a launchd timer is plenty). The payoff is that git log over your memory directory is a real history of what your agents learned and when they changed their minds.

Git gives you the knowledge with a history. It deliberately leaves out the other half - sessions, tasks, trials, events - which is what seamlessd export is for. They compose: git for the diffable record of what your agents learned, an archive for the whole instance.

The whole instance in one archive

seamlessd export
# wrote /Users/you/seamless-nuc.local-20260923T220501Z.tar.gz (4.1 MiB)
#   host nuc.local, seamlessd 0.9.1, created 2026-09-23T22:05:01Z
#   corpus: 214 memories, 38 notes
#   database: schema v25, 18422 rows across 21 tables

One gzipped tar with the markdown corpus, a consistent snapshot of seam.db, and a manifest describing what is inside. Full flags in the CLI reference.

Three things worth knowing:

  • Run it while the daemon is up. The snapshot is SQLite's VACUUM INTO, taken inside a read transaction, so a write in flight is simply not in it. No cp of a WAL-mode database, no stopping anything. (A plain cp of seam.db under a live writer can capture a torn state; this cannot.)
  • The key is not in it. Config and mcp.api_key are deliberately excluded, so an archive can go to a NAS or another machine without carrying this machine's only credential.
  • - streams. seamlessd export -o - | ssh backup-box 'cat > seam.tgz' writes the archive to stdout and the report to stderr.

--no-db gives you a knowledge-only archive: the two markdown trees, nothing else. It is the tarball equivalent of the git recipe above.

Restore

seamlessd backups                                           # what there is to restore
seamlessd restore seamless-nuc.local-20260923T030000Z-auto.tar.gz
seamlessd restore --merge ~/Downloads/seamless.tar.gz       # bring back only what is missing

seamlessd restore is the console's restore from a terminal. Name a backup as seamlessd backups lists it, or give any backup file's path. It says what the backup holds and asks before it changes anything (--yes skips the question). Without --merge the backup replaces all data and today's is saved as a before-restore backup first, so restoring that one undoes it. With --merge only what the backup has and this install lacks is added. Either way it keeps what a console restore keeps: locks, passkeys, project privacy, repo routes and console settings.

There is nothing to stop first. With the daemon running, the command prepares the restore, the daemon restarts to finish it, and the command waits for the result. With no daemon, it applies the restore itself.

seamlessd restore needs a database to restore into, so on a machine where Seamless has never run, start it once first (the installer does). It refuses a database older than its own binary, like every one-shot command.

Restoring with seamlessd import

seamlessd import is the older, lower-level way. It brings the backup's own passkeys and console settings with it, which seamlessd restore never does:

seamlessd stop
mv ~/.seamless ~/.seamless.old                   # import restores only into an empty data directory
seamlessd import --from seamless-nuc.local-20260923T220501Z.tar.gz
seamlessd doctor && seamlessd start

Into an empty data directory, that is a restore: every .md lands byte-for-byte and the database snapshot is renamed into place last. Into a populated one it is a merge instead, first-writer-wins by ULID. Which one it will be is a property of the destination, is printed in the report, and cannot be overridden - so there is no way to ask for a restore and get a populated instance wiped. Add --dry-run to see the mode and the counts without writing anything.

A restore refuses while a daemon is answering for that data directory (it would be replacing seam.db underneath it) and names seamlessd stop; --force overrides. A merge does not need the daemon down.

You can also restore the knowledge alone, from an archive or from git:

# files back in place
cp -R backup/memory backup/notes ~/.seamless/
make run

Startup reconciliation walks the tree, notices which files the index does not know about (or whose content hash changed), and indexes them. A file watcher keeps it in sync from then on. You do not run a reindex command, because there isn't one to forget.

To force a full rebuild, stop the daemon, delete seam.db, and start it again. You lose sessions, tasks, trials, and events; you lose no knowledge.

Locked projects

A backup keeps a locked project locked. Every backup and seamlessd export records every locked project in the archive, whether the console set the lock or peer_auth.force_locked holds it, and a --no-db archive records them too. The file itself is not encrypted, so a lock does not protect it: keep the archive as carefully as the most sensitive project in it.

With seamlessd restore or the console there is nothing to choose: the restore keeps today's locks and passkeys and adds the backup's locks. The rest of this section is about seamlessd import.

Before an import writes anything, it looks for a passkey that can open those projects:

  • Restoring into an empty data directory, the backup's passkeys come back with its database. One counts if it was enrolled for this instance's relying party and can reach this machine: a synced passkey, a security key or a phone, or any passkey when you restore on the machine that enrolled it.
  • Merging, this instance's own passkeys count. A merge never brings passkeys.

If it finds one, it asks whether you still have it. If it finds none, or you don't, you choose:

  • Keep the locks and add a passkey right after. The import prints the steps. The Approvers page takes a new passkey with a one-time code from your terminal, so a passkey you no longer have does not lock you out.
  • Add a passkey first, on a merge. The import stops with nothing changed. A restore doesn't offer this, because a daemon started on the empty data directory would create a database and turn the restore into a merge.
  • Remove the locks from these projects. They keep their isolation setting, and agents working in them then read them without asking.

With no terminal to ask on, an import that finds no passkey stops with nothing changed until you pass --keep-locks or --remove-locks. Add --dry-run to see what it finds.

Once the daemon is running, check the passkey for real by unlocking one of the projects with it at /console/unlock/<project>. Only a browser and the authenticator can prove you still have it, so the import can't.

A few details:

  • A lock held by the old machine's force_locked list becomes a console lock here, because no archive carries a config. If this machine's config force locks the project too, the file keeps holding it.
  • With peer_auth off, locks do nothing, so the import says so and asks. Turn it on before you start the daemon.
  • A merge that brings locks needs the daemon stopped, because a daemon reads the locked projects when it starts. --force overrides that, and you must then restart the daemon right away.
  • On a merge, a project that is open here and locked in the archive is raised to the archive's isolation setting, and leaves any family or parent it had. If it has child projects it can't be fenced, so the import stops with nothing changed.
  • --remove-locks removes the archive's locks only. A force lock in this config, or a lock this instance already had, stays.
  • A restore puts things back as they stood at the backup. A lock set later isn't in it, and a passkey removed later returns: check seamlessd approvers list.

Merging two instances

Importing an archive into an instance that already has data is a merge, and it is idempotent: anything whose ULID is already here is skipped, so running the same archive twice inserts zero the second time. That makes it the way to fold a laptop's instance into a desktop's, or several devices' into one.

Two rules keep it honest:

  • Collisions are reported, never resolved. A memory whose path is already held by a different item is left unwritten and both ids are printed; a session name or project slug already taken is reported rather than renamed. Deciding which one wins is yours.
  • This machine's settings stay this machine's. Repo mappings, families, briefing overrides, and the embedder switch are not merged, and neither are embeddings - vectors belong to whichever model you run here, so imported items are embedded on write instead.

Import from Seam v1

seamlessd import --from ~/.seam

seamlessd import fronts two operations and picks between them by what --from names on disk: a directory is a Seam v1 store, a file (or -) is an archive. Point it at a v1 data directory and it brings that store's memories, sessions, and tool-call events into seam.db. It is idempotent: running it twice does not double anything, so a partial import is safe to re-run.

Hand-editing

Files are the source of truth, so editing them by hand is allowed and expected - the watcher picks up your change and reindexes it.

Two rules:

  1. Never hand-stamp invalid_at or superseded_by. Those are set by the supersede path, which also updates the indexes and the pointer between the two memories. Writing them by hand produces a file that says one thing and a database that believes another, and the lifecycle invariants (stamp once, point only at an active memory, never self-supersede) stop being true. Use memory_write with supersedes - see Memory & notes.
  2. Do not hand-edit id. It is a ULID assigned once and referenced by superseded_by pointers elsewhere.

Everything else - the body, the description, tags, the kind - is yours to edit in any text editor.

Moving machines

# on the old machine
seamlessd export -o seamless.tar.gz

# on the new one, once Seamless is installed and has started
seamlessd restore ~/seamless.tar.gz

Every memory and note comes back byte-for-byte, with the sessions, tasks, trials, and events. Backups in a synced folder work the same way: point the new machine's backup folder at it, and its backups are in the console's list, marked as from another Seamless. If you are folding the old machine into an instance that already has data, add --merge - see Merging two instances.

The new machine keeps its own settings, as every restore does: its passkeys, its repo routes (a session started in a repository maps it again by its directory name, and seamlessd map-repo points one at another project) and its console settings. Locked projects come back locked. To open them, enroll a passkey here: the Approvers page takes one with a one-time code from your terminal. To bring the old machine's passkeys and console settings across too, restore with seamlessd import into an empty data directory instead (Restoring with seamlessd import).

The install generates a fresh mcp.api_key rather than copying the old config: the key is the only credential, it is deliberately not in the archive, and a machine migration is a good moment not to spread it around. See Install & deploy.

If all you want is the knowledge, the git recipe moves it just as well (git clone <remote> ~/.seamless), and so does seamlessd export --no-db. The index rebuilds itself on first start either way.
